title: Trump Tries Again to Change Who Gets to Be a U.S. Citizen at Birth
summary: Imagine being born in a hospital in New York City, but the government says you can't be an American. That's what President Trump's new orders could mean for some babies. On Thursday, he signed two executive orders that try to limit birthright citizenship — the rule that says almost everyone born on U.S. soil is automatically a citizen. This is his second try. The Supreme Court already struck down his first attempt in June. Trump says these new orders are "adjusted" to fit the court's decision, but many experts think they'll end up in court again. The 14th Amendment to the Constitution promises citizenship to people born here, with very few exceptions. Right now, babies of foreign diplomats don't get citizenship. Trump's orders would expand that list. One order says babies born to parents who came to the U.S. just to give birth — called "birth tourism" — won't be citizens. The other order targets children of anyone working at a foreign embassy, the United Nations, or other international groups. It even includes kids of parents linked to groups the U.S. calls terrorist organizations, like Antifa or Tren de Aragua. But how would the government know if a parent is in one of those groups? Law professor César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández says those groups don't share member lists. He also points out that the Constitution never mentions surrogacy, so a rule about babies born through surrogates raises brand-new legal questions. How big is birth tourism? Numbers are fuzzy. The CDC says about 9,600 babies were born to foreign moms with addresses outside the U.S. in 2024. Another group guesses 20,000 to 26,000 per year. Trump's order calls it a huge problem, but experts say the real numbers are much smaller. For now, the orders are just words on paper. Courts will likely decide if they can actually change who gets to call themselves an American.
why_it_matters: If the rules changed, some kids born in U.S. hospitals might not be citizens, which could affect where they can go to school, live, or even travel with their families.

background_read: The 14th Amendment was added to the U.S. Constitution after the Civil War in 1868 to make sure former slaves and their children would be full citizens. For over 150 years it has meant that almost every baby born on American soil is a U.S. citizen.

President Donald Trump (who returned to office in 2025) has long talked about ending automatic citizenship for children of people who are not permanent residents. The Supreme Court (the top court in the U.S.) has already rejected one of his earlier attempts.
The idea of "birth tourism" — when someone travels to the U.S. just to have a baby — has been debated for years, but experts say it happens far less than some leaders claim.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Trump, along with legal experts like César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández and groups like Antifa and Tren de Aragua mentioned in the orders.
WHAT: Two executive orders that try to expand the list of babies who do not get U.S. citizenship at birth, even if born on U.S. soil.
WHERE: The article does not specify a signing location, but presidential orders are typically signed in Washington, D.C.
WHY: Trump says the country needs to stop "birth tourism" and close loopholes used by people he considers dangerous, but critics say the changes clash with the 14th Amendment.
